standard.title: Subjective and objective language
standard.description: identify the subjective language of opinion and feeling, and the objective language of factual reporting
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand how evaluative and emotive language including modal verbs can vary in forcefulness (AC9E3LA02). They have not yet distinguished subjective language of opinion/feeling from objective language of factual reporting as distinct registers with different purposes.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can identify subjective language (opinion, feeling, thinking verbs) and objective language (factual reporting, summary verbs) in texts, explain the different purposes each serves, and recognise when each is appropriate.

nodes.label: Language of opinion and feeling
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify thinking verbs and emotive vocabulary that signal a subjective point of view in a text.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify thinking verbs (e.g. 'I think', 'I believe', 'I feel') in a provided text and explain that these signal the writer's personal view.
nodes.typical_width: Identify a range of subjective language features across texts — thinking verbs, emotive adjectives, evaluative adverbs — and explain how these position the reader to share or consider the author's viewpoint.
wider: Compare the use of subjective language across different opinion text types — a review, a letter to the editor, a persuasive speech — and identify which features are consistent and which vary by genre
Explore how First Nations Australian authors use subjective voice to position readers in relation to cultural knowledge and experience
nodes.hinge_reason: Identifying objective language in N2 requires students to know what subjective features look like — the contrast between thinking verbs/emotive vocabulary (N1) and summary verbs/neutral vocabulary (N2) is how students distinguish the two registers.

response_modes.reason: Subjective language features vary widely across opinion text types — students need multiple examples before the pattern is distinguishable from genre-specific features, and before the subjective/objective contrast is reliably seen.

success_criteria: Can identify at least two thinking verbs in a text and explain that they signal personal opinion
Can distinguish emotive vocabulary (e.g. 'wonderful', 'terrible') from neutral descriptors

nodes.label: Language of factual reporting
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify summary verbs and neutral vocabulary that signal objective, factual reporting in a text.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify summary verbs (e.g. 'we concluded', 'the report found', 'results showed') in a provided text and explain that these signal reported facts rather than personal views.
nodes.typical_width: Identify objective language features across informational texts — summary verbs, precise nouns, impersonal constructions, present tense for facts — and explain how these create an effect of factual authority.
wider: Compare how objective language is used differently in scientific reports, news articles and encyclopaedia entries — same information, different degrees of formality
Examine how news reporting attempts objectivity and identify moments where subjective language creeps in
nodes.hinge_reason: N3's explanation of why writers choose each register requires students to accurately characterise what each register consists of — the misconception about objective language from N2 produces inaccurate purpose analysis in N3.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly conflate objective language with 'no adjectives' or 'short sentences'. Precision about what objective language features are — summary verbs, impersonal constructions — requires consolidation through multiple examples.

success_criteria: Can identify at least one summary verb and explain that it reports a finding rather than expressing an opinion
Can distinguish 'The man has 6 cats' (objective) from 'The man has too many noisy cats' (subjective) and name the feature that marks each

nodes.label: Purpose and context of each register
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why writers choose subjective or objective language depending on the purpose and context of their text.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain why a particular text uses subjective or objective language by linking the language choice to the text's purpose.
nodes.typical_width: Compare two texts on similar topics — one subjective (review, opinion piece), one objective (report, news article) — and explain how the purpose of each text drives its language choices.
wider: Analyse a text that mixes subjective and objective language (e.g. a persuasive essay using reported evidence) and explain why the author moves between registers
Write a short objective and subjective version of the same information about a familiar topic, then discuss the effect of each on the reader

response_modes.reason: Students often assume all informational texts should be objective and all personal texts subjective. Mixed-register texts — persuasive essays, biographies — help students see that purpose, not text type alone, determines register.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The interplay between subjective and objective language in real texts is rich territory — opinion pieces that use objective evidence, reports that reveal authorial bias. Wider engagement builds sophisticated register awareness.
success_criteria: Can explain why a specific text uses the register it does by naming its purpose
Does not assume that only reports are objective — can identify register choices in any text type
